newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Ageing babyboomers to hit U.S. budget.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ageing babyboomers to hit U.S. budget.

text.p: Democratic and Republican candidates have pledged to balance the budget, in the red for 58 of the last 66 years, but a wave of retiring baby boomers could break their promises early in the next century.

Between 2008 and 2011, the "baby boomers" will become eligible for Social Security, start receiving Medicare benefits and straining the Medicaid programme, says Robert Reischauer, a senior fellow at The Brookings Institution.
Despite that, many politicians from both parties are so confident they can balance the budget every year starting in 2002 they support a constitutional amendment requiring it.
But budget analysts say it is important to do the right kind of deficit reduction now if balance is to be achieved.

These analysts challenge the sunny promises of President Bill Clinton, Republican challenger Bob Dole and congressional candidates from both political parties, who proclaim a balanced budget is in reach even if tax cuts are offered.
Republicans passed tax cuts in Congress last year but Clinton refused to sign them into law. Nevertheless Clinton has proposed tax cuts of his own for child and educational costs.
TAX CUTS A CENTREPIECE OF DOLE'S CAMPAIGN
Congressional Democrats endorse Clinton's tax cuts and have a list of their own. While Dole has made the centrepiece of his campaign a 15 percent cut in income tax rates.

Budget experts acknowledge it may be possible to balance the budget with tax cuts in 2002 by using one-time measures, such as the sales of federal assets. But the budget would soon tip out of balance and the deficit would grow again.

"Deficits will start to mount rapidly" around 2010, the non-partisan Congressional Budget Office (CBO) said earlier this year, because the ageing baby boom generation will leave behind fewer people to work and pay taxes.
The pressure of entitlements "could put an end to the upward trend in living standards that the nation has long enjoyed," the CBO said.
Some optimists in both parties count on economic growth to solve problems, short- and long-term.

Republican vice-presidential candidate Jack Kemp, a long-time believer in tax cuts, says Dole's $548 billion in tax cuts, combined with some spending cuts, will spur enough growth to balance the budget.
"You cannot balance the budget...without growing the economy," he said in a nationally televised debate with Vice- President Al Gore.
House Democratic leader Richard Gephardt agrees with him up to a point.
"We need to grow this economy and grow out of the deficit and we can do it" with three percent growth, said the Missouri Democrat. "I'm with Jack Kemp on that much of it."

But the Clinton adminstration and the non-partisan Congressional Budget Office estimate real growth in the coming decade will hover between 2.1 and 2.3 percent. Joseph Stiglitz, chairman of the President's Council of Economic Advisers, said the economy may grow faster but he is not ready to change his projections.
Growth or no growth, spending cuts are also required in the next few years. Dole and Clinton promise to cut spending but have not said exactly what they will cut.

Dole has promised to avoid touching Social Security, the military or Medicare and cannot cut interest on the national debt. Those are the four most costly items in the budget, accounting for two-thirds of spending.
Dole says he will cut what's left, snipping it by five percent. The Centre for Budget and Policy Priorities estimates such cuts must average 37 percent.
Brookings' Reischauer, a former CBO director, says small changes in discretionary items is the wrong approach. He advocates tackling the tougher entitlements spending areas.
Reischauer suggests trimming cost-of-living adjustments for Social Security and requiring workers to save one to two percent of their income in Individual Retirement Accounts.

Stiglitz, Democratic congressional leaders and Dole advocate a commission to tackle the problem, citing the success of a Social Security Commission in the early 1980s. But commissions do not necessarily make a difference.
Another Social Security panel, which was supposed to report last year, has been split over the role privately-directed investment should play. It is unclear when the report will come out.

Democratic Senator Robert Kerrey of Nebraska co-chaired another commission on the rising cost of entitlements, only to see its recommendations shelved after it came out in late 1994. Kerrey says it is time to act.
He wants to expand Medicare to cover all uninsured workers and force everyone to pay a bigger chunk of health care to make them aware of the costs.

The administration has made some stabs at looking at the long-term problem. Clinton's budget released early this year says capping per capita costs is a solution to Medicaid, which pays the costs of nursing homes for the elderly.

And the administration expresses optimism Medicare costs can be held down as well, although it is vague about exactly how that will be done. Medicare per capita costs, the budget says, "are assumed to slow down gradually".
Stiglitz says it is tough to come up with precise long-term health-care solutions now because technology is changing quickly and cost increases are erratic.
"I don't think anyone responsible would have confidence in precise projections 15 years from now," he said.
